manifest.title: Flocks, Herds, and Schools: A Distributed Behavioral Model

claims.paraphrase: A flock's motion is the result of many birds each following simple behaviours.

anchor.quote: The aggregate motion of the simulated flock is the result of the dense interaction of the relatively simple behaviors of the individual simulated birds.

claims.paraphrase: The model is distributed: no bird leads, each chooses its own course.

anchor.quote: The aggregate motion of the simulated flock is created by a distributed behavioral model much like that at work in a natural flock; the birds choose their own course.

claims.paraphrase: A bird in a large flock perceives only part of it: what is near it.

anchor.quote: an individual bird must have a localized and filtered perception of the rest of the flock.

claims.paraphrase: Flocking depends on each bird's limited, local view.

anchor.quote: the aggregate motion that we intuitively recognize as "flocking" (or schooling or herding) depends upon a limited, localized view of the world.

claims.paraphrase: Every behaviour is stated in terms of the flockmates near a bird.

anchor.quote: The behaviors that make up the flocking model are stated in terms of "nearby flockmates."

claims.paraphrase: The first behaviour: avoid colliding with nearby flockmates.

anchor.quote: 1. Collision Avoidance: avoid collisions with nearby flockmates

claims.paraphrase: The second behaviour: match the velocity of nearby flockmates.

anchor.quote: 2. Velocity Matching: attempt to match velocity with nearby flockmates

claims.paraphrase: The third behaviour: stay close to nearby flockmates.

anchor.quote: 3. Flock Centering: attempt to stay close to nearby flockmates

claims.paraphrase: Collision avoidance reads where flockmates are, not how they move.

anchor.quote: Static collision avoidance is based on the relative position of the flockmates and ignores their velocity.

claims.paraphrase: Real flocks split to pass an obstacle, and a model must too.

anchor.quote: Real flocks sometimes split apart to go around an obstacle.

claims.paraphrase: Flocks join, and around obstacles a large flock can split into smaller ones.

anchor.quote: Solitary boids and smaller flocks join to become larger flocks, and in the presence of external obstacles (discussed below), larger flocks can split into smaller flocks.

claims.paraphrase: Avoiding an obstacle is planned early, not corrected at the last moment.

anchor.quote: avoiding an obstacle should involve long-range planning rather than panicky corrections at the last minute.

claims.paraphrase: Avoiding an obstacle can override flock centering for a time.

anchor.quote: the flock centering urge could be correctly ignored temporarily in favor of a maneuver to avoid a static obstacle.
